scenarios.title: Planning Your Study Path
scenarios.situation: You have 3 weeks before your Docker interview/exam. You've just opened this bootcamp with 15 domains ahead of you.
scenarios.prompt: What is the most effective study sequence?
choices: Start Here lessons → core domains in order → Systems Anatomy → Mock Assessment → Capstone, doing drills daily
Jump straight to the Mock Assessment to see where you stand
Study only your weakest domain until it's perfect, then move on
Read all lessons first, then do all scenarios, then all labs
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. The bootcamp is sequenced deliberately: orientation first, then progressive domain mastery with interleaved drills for retention, Systems Anatomy to connect it all, mock under realistic conditions, capstone to prove it. Jumping to the mock wastes its diagnostic value; perfecting one domain starves the others; batching by activity type kills interleaving benefits.
scenarios.hint: What does each phase prepare you for? What happens if you skip the foundation?

scenarios.title: The Passive Reader Trap
scenarios.situation: A learner has 'completed' 40 lessons but fails every scenario. They read each lesson carefully and passed all knowledge checks on the first try.
scenarios.prompt: What went wrong, and what's the fix?
choices: They consumed passively without application — the fix is interleaving scenarios immediately after lessons and doing teach-backs aloud
The lessons are too easy — skip to harder material
They need to re-read the lessons more carefully
Knowledge checks are broken — report a bug
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Passing knowledge checks proves recognition, not application. Scenarios demand transfer — using knowledge in novel situations. The fix is structural: never finish a lesson without immediately attempting its scenarios, and explain each concept aloud (teach-back) to expose shallow understanding.
scenarios.hint: What's the difference between recognizing an answer and producing one under pressure?

scenarios.title: COPY or ADD?
scenarios.situation: A Dockerfile uses ADD for everything: copying source files, fetching a tarball from a URL, and adding a config file. A reviewer flags this in code review.
scenarios.prompt: What is the best-practice guidance, and why?
evidence:
ADD https://example.com/data.tar.gz /opt/
ADD app/ /app/
ADD config.yaml /app/
choices: Use COPY for local files — ADD's magic (URL fetch, tar auto-extract) makes builds surprising; reserve ADD for when you actually need it
Use ADD for everything — it's a superset of COPY so it's always better
Replace both with RUN curl — COPY and ADD are deprecated
It doesn't matter — they produce identical layers
scenarios.why: COPY does one transparent thing: copy local files. ADD additionally fetches remote URLs and auto-extracts archives, which hurts build-cache predictability and clarity. Best practice: COPY by default, ADD only when you need its extra behaviors (and even URL fetching is often clearer as an explicit RUN curl with checksum verification).
scenarios.hint: Which instruction does exactly one obvious thing?

scenarios.title: The container that ignores arguments
scenarios.situation: Your image sets CMD ["--port", "8080"]. Running 'docker run myimg --port 9090' doesn't change the port — the container still listens on 8080.
scenarios.prompt: What is wrong, and how do CMD and ENTRYPOINT interact?
choices: ENTRYPOINT's exec list already hardcodes --port 8080, so the CMD arguments are appended after it — move the port flag out of ENTRYPOINT or use CMD as the default args
CMD is ignored whenever ENTRYPOINT exists — delete the CMD line
docker run arguments override ENTRYPOINT, not CMD — use --entrypoint instead
Arguments after the image name are ignored by design
scenarios.why: With exec-form ENTRYPOINT, 'docker run <image> <args>' appends <args> to the ENTRYPOINT — replacing CMD entirely. Here the final command becomes 'python app.py --port 8080 --port 9090', and the app takes the first flag. The idiomatic split: ENTRYPOINT ["python", "app.py"] (the fixed executable) + CMD ["--port", "8080"] (default args, overridable).
scenarios.hint: What is the final command line when both ENTRYPOINT and run-args are present?

scenarios.title: Every build reinstalls the world
scenarios.situation: Your Node.js Dockerfile copies the whole repo, then runs npm ci. Every one-line code change triggers a full dependency reinstall — builds take 9 minutes.
scenarios.prompt: How do you restructure the Dockerfile to cache dependencies?
evidence:
FROM node:20
WORKDIR /app
COPY . .
RUN npm ci
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
choices: COPY package.json package-lock.json first, RUN npm ci, then COPY the rest — dependency layer is cached until manifests change
Add --no-cache to the build so layers are always fresh
Combine COPY and RUN into a single layer to reduce layer count
Move npm ci before FROM so it runs only once ever
scenarios.why: Docker caches each layer and invalidates everything after the first changed instruction. Copying package manifests first means the expensive npm ci layer is reused whenever only application code changes. Layer count barely matters; cache invalidation order is everything.
scenarios.hint: Which changes more often — your dependencies or your code?

scenarios.title: The 1.2 GB frontend image
scenarios.situation: Your React app's image is 1.2 GB because the final image contains the Node toolchain, build tools, and source maps — but at runtime it only needs nginx serving static files.
scenarios.prompt: Which Dockerfile technique shrinks this, and how?
choices: Multi-stage build: a builder stage compiles the app, then COPY --from=builder the dist/ output into a slim nginx stage
Use a bigger base image so compression is more efficient
Delete node_modules in a RUN step at the end of the single stage
Push the big image — registries deduplicate the toolchain automatically
scenarios.why: Multi-stage builds let you use heavy tooling in an early stage and copy only artifacts into the final minimal stage (e.g., nginx:alpine). Deleting files in a later RUN doesn't shrink the image — the earlier layer still contains them. The result is often 10–50x smaller with a reduced attack surface.
scenarios.hint: Do the build tools need to exist in the image that actually runs?

scenarios.title: Secrets shipped in the image
scenarios.situation: A teammate builds with 'COPY . .' and you discover the image contains .env (production secrets), .git history, and node_modules. Anyone who pulls the image can extract them.
scenarios.prompt: What is the immediate fix, and the deeper lesson?
choices: Add a .dockerignore excluding .env, .git, node_modules — and rotate the exposed secrets, since they're already in image history
Add .dockerignore — that retroactively removes secrets from already-pushed images
Switch to ADD, which skips hidden files automatically
It's fine — image layers are encrypted in registries
scenarios.why: .dockerignore keeps unwanted files out of the build context (faster builds, smaller images, fewer leaks). But .dockerignore can't un-ship what's already pushed — layers are immutable and downloadable, so any exposed secret must be rotated. Deeper lesson: secrets never belong in build contexts; inject at runtime.
scenarios.hint: Can you un-publish a layer that already left your machine?

scenarios.title: Latest isn't latest
scenarios.situation: Production runs image: 'payments:latest'. After a deploy, some hosts run the new code and some run code from three weeks ago — all reporting tag 'latest'.
scenarios.prompt: What went wrong, and what tagging discipline fixes it?
choices: 'latest' is just a mutable tag — hosts that didn't pull kept the old image; pin immutable tags (e.g., payments:2.4.1 or a digest) so every host runs the identical artifact
The registry served stale data — switch registries
Docker caches 'latest' forever — you must use docker pull --force
Tags are content-addressed, so this is impossible — the hosts must be misconfigured
scenarios.why: 'latest' is a floating pointer, not a version guarantee: a host only updates it when it pulls, and pull policies vary. Immutable tags (semver, git SHA) or digests (sha256:...) make 'which exact bytes are running' unambiguous and rollbacks safe. Only tags are mutable; digests are content-addressed.
scenarios.hint: What does the tag 'latest' actually point to on a host that hasn't pulled in weeks?

scenarios.title: Slow Rebuilds
scenarios.situation: A Node.js Dockerfile copies the whole project, then runs `npm ci`, then copies source again. Every one-line code change triggers a full 4-minute dependency reinstall.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct layer-ordering fix?
evidence:
FROM node:20-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY . .
RUN npm ci
COPY src/ ./src/
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
choices: Copy `package.json`/`package-lock.json` first, run `npm ci`, then copy the rest of the source — Docker caches each layer, so unchanged dependency layers are reused and only the source layer rebuilds
Add `--no-cache` to every build so layers never go stale
Combine everything into a single RUN line to reduce the layer count
Use `COPY . .` twice so Docker has two chances to cache
scenarios.why: Docker caches layers by instruction + file contents. Putting the volatile `COPY . .` before `npm ci` invalidates the dependency layer on every code change. Ordering from least-changed (dependency manifests) to most-changed (source) maximizes cache hits. `--no-cache` would make things slower, not faster.
scenarios.hint: Which files change on every commit, and which almost never change? Which should Docker see first?

scenarios.title: Bloated Production Image
scenarios.situation: A Go service's production image is 1.1GB because the Dockerfile builds from `golang:1.22` and ships the toolchain, source, and build cache. Security flags it: too much attack surface.
scenarios.prompt: What is the best remediation?
evidence:
FROM golang:1.22
WORKDIR /app
COPY . .
RUN go build -o server .
CMD ["./server"]
choices: Convert to a multi-stage build: compile in the `golang` stage, then `COPY --from=builder` only the binary into a minimal runtime stage (`scratch` or `distroless`) — the final image contains just the binary
Add a `.dockerignore` excluding `*.go` files; the binary doesn't need source
Switch the base to `golang:1.22-alpine`; Alpine is small enough for production
Run `docker image prune` on the registry to shrink the stored image
scenarios.why: Multi-stage builds separate build-time dependencies from the runtime image. Only artifacts explicitly copied with `COPY --from=` land in the final stage, so the toolchain, module cache, and source never ship. A Go static binary on `scratch` is typically <20MB — smaller, faster to pull, and with far less attack surface. `.dockerignore` helps build context, not image contents.
scenarios.hint: Which stage's filesystem ends up in the final image — and what from the build stage actually needs to be there?

scenarios.title: The 2 GB Build Context
scenarios.situation: Every `docker build` starts with `Sending build context to Docker daemon (2.1 GB)` and takes minutes before the first step even runs. The repo contains a `.git` directory, node_modules, and test fixtures.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct fix?
choices: Add a `.dockerignore` excluding `.git`, `node_modules`, fixtures, and other unneeded paths — the context sent to the daemon shrinks to megabytes and builds start instantly
Run `docker build --no-cache` so the context is rebuilt fresh each time
Move the Dockerfile into a subdirectory; the context follows the Dockerfile
Increase the daemon's memory limit so it can ingest the 2 GB context faster
scenarios.why: The build context is everything under the build directory minus .dockerignore — it is tarred and sent to the daemon on every build. A bloated context wastes time and invalidation. .dockerignore is the standard fix; --no-cache makes things slower.
scenarios.hint: What is actually being sent to the daemon before step 1 runs?

scenarios.title: Naming the image for the registry
scenarios.situation: You built 'myapp:1.0' locally and need to push it to registry.example.com/team-a. 'docker push myapp:1.0' fails.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct tag-and-push sequence?
choices: docker tag myapp:1.0 registry.example.com/team-a/myapp:1.0, then docker push registry.example.com/team-a/myapp:1.0
docker push myapp:1.0 --registry registry.example.com
Rename the Dockerfile — image names are fixed at build time
docker push automatically prefixes the configured default registry
scenarios.why: The registry hostname must be part of the image name: [registry/][namespace/]name:tag. 'docker tag' creates the fully-qualified alias pointing at the same image ID, then push sends it to that registry. Without the prefix, Docker assumes Docker Hub.
scenarios.hint: How does the push command know which registry to contact?

scenarios.title: Unauthorized on pull
scenarios.situation: CI can push to your private registry, but a new cluster node fails 'docker pull' with 'unauthorized: authentication required'.
scenarios.prompt: What is missing, and where does Docker keep the credential?
choices: The node isn't logged in — run 'docker login registry.example.com'; credentials are stored (preferably via a credential helper) in ~/.docker/config.json
Pulls are anonymous by default — the registry is misconfigured
Private registries don't support pull — only push
Rebuild the image publicly — private pulls aren't a thing
scenarios.why: 'docker login' authenticates and stores credentials in ~/.docker/config.json (use a credential helper like docker-credential-pass instead of base64 plaintext where possible). Every host that pulls private images needs its own login — or better, a registry credential wired into the orchestrator (e.g., imagePullSecrets in K8s).
scenarios.hint: What did CI do that the new node hasn't?

scenarios.title: The tag moved under us
scenarios.situation: You deployed 'registry.example.com/team-a/myapp:1.0' everywhere. The image team re-pushed a fixed image under the same 1.0 tag; half your fleet has the old bytes, half the new.
scenarios.prompt: How do you make deployments byte-identical?
choices: Pin the digest: myapp:1.0@sha256:<digest> — digests are content-addressed and immutable
Use the 'latest' tag — it always resolves to the newest
Tags are immutable — the image team broke the rules
Add a timestamp to the tag on every deploy
scenarios.why: Tags are mutable pointers; digests (sha256 of the manifest) identify exact content. 'image:tag@sha256:digest' pins bytes precisely — pulls always resolve identically. 'docker images --digests' shows them. Tag immutability policies in the registry (Harbor/ECR support them) prevent the re-push problem at the source.
scenarios.hint: Which reference can't change out from under you?

scenarios.title: Choosing a registry
scenarios.situation: Your company needs a registry with RBAC, image scanning, and retention policies for 20 teams. Docker Hub's free tier won't cover it.
scenarios.prompt: What are the realistic options?
choices: Self-hosted Harbor, or cloud registries (ECR, GCR/Artifact Registry, ACR) — all offer private repos, RBAC, scanning, and retention
Docker Hub is the only registry Docker can use
Store images on NFS — registries are optional
Email tarballs from 'docker save' — simplest for 20 teams
scenarios.why: Docker works with any OCI-compliant registry. Harbor (open source, self-hosted) adds RBAC, vulnerability scanning (Trivy), retention/tag-immutability policies, and replication. Cloud registries integrate with IAM and are managed. docker save/load tarballs are for air-gapped transfer, not team workflows.
scenarios.hint: Is the Docker client locked to Docker Hub?

scenarios.title: toomanyrequests at 9 AM
scenarios.situation: Every morning CI fails with 'toomanyrequests: You have reached your pull rate limit' from Docker Hub. Nothing changed in your Dockerfiles.
scenarios.prompt: What is happening, and what are the fixes?
choices: Anonymous/free-tier pull rate limits — authenticate pulls, use a pull-through cache/mirror, or vendor base images into your own registry
Docker Hub is down — wait it out
Your images are too large — shrink them to avoid the limit
Rate limits apply per image — rename your images
scenarios.why: Docker Hub rate-limits pulls (stricter for anonymous users; limits are per IP/account per time window). Fixes: 'docker login' for higher authenticated limits, run a pull-through cache registry mirror, or copy base images into your own registry/ECR so CI doesn't hit Hub at all. Authenticated limits are per-account, so use a dedicated CI service account.
scenarios.hint: What changed at 9 AM — your Dockerfiles, or how many pulls happen?

scenarios.title: Disk full of old images
scenarios.situation: A build server's disk is 95% full. 'docker images' shows hundreds of untagged '<none>' images and old app versions.
scenarios.prompt: How do you reclaim space safely?
choices: 'docker image prune -a' removes unused images (dangling and unreferenced); add filters or run per-project cleanup in CI to keep it routine
'docker rmi $(docker images -q)' — removes everything including running containers' images
Delete /var/lib/docker directly — fastest
Images don't take disk space — look elsewhere
scenarios.why: 'docker image prune' removes dangling images; '-a' also removes images not used by any container. 'docker system prune' goes further (containers, networks, build cache — add --volumes only if you mean it). Never rm -rf /var/lib/docker while the daemon runs — it corrupts state. Schedule pruning in CI to prevent recurrence.
scenarios.hint: Which prune flag distinguishes 'dangling' from 'unused'?

scenarios.title: Registry Push Denied
scenarios.situation: CI builds the image fine but `docker push registry.example.com/team/app:v1` fails with `denied: requested access to the resource is denied`. The same pipeline pushed last week.
scenarios.prompt: What is the most likely cause and fix?
evidence:
=> pushing layers... 
ERROR: denied: requested access to the resource is denied
repository exists; CI identity has push rights per IAM policy
choices: The CI credential expired or lost its push grant (rotated token, expired service-account key) — re-authenticate (`docker login` with a fresh credential) and verify the identity still holds push permission on that repository path
The image tag `v1` is immutable; registries reject overwriting tags
Docker Hub rate limits block pushes after too many pulls
The image must be pushed with `docker push --force`; registries require confirmation for overwrites
scenarios.why: `denied: requested access to the resource is denied` is an authorization failure at push time, not a build problem. The classic causes: expired/rotated credentials in CI secrets, or the token's scope narrowed to pull-only. Re-authenticating with a fresh credential and confirming repository-level push rights resolves it. Tags are mutable by default in most registries.
scenarios.hint: The build succeeded and the repository exists. Which step — proving who you are, or being allowed — is failing?

scenarios.title: First compose file
scenarios.situation: You need a web app + Postgres locally: app built from ./app, Postgres 16 with a password, app port 8080 → 80, data persisted.
scenarios.prompt: What are the essential compose.yaml pieces?
choices: services: with build:/image:, ports:, environment:/env_file:, volumes: for data; a named volume for postgres; 'docker compose up -d'
A Dockerfile per service is enough — compose is automatic
version: '3' is required or compose fails
Each service needs its own compose.yaml file
scenarios.why: compose.yaml declares services (build context or image, ports, env, volumes, depends_on), plus top-level networks:/volumes: as needed. Named volumes persist DB data across 'compose down'. The 'version:' key is obsolete (ignored with a warning). One file, one 'docker compose up -d' (the hyphen-less v2 CLI).
scenarios.hint: Which top-level keys describe the app, its data, and its networking?

scenarios.title: App starts before the DB is ready
scenarios.situation: compose has 'depends_on: [db]' but the app still crashes on boot — Postgres is starting but not accepting connections yet.
scenarios.prompt: Why doesn't depends_on fix this, and what does?
choices: depends_on orders startup, not readiness — add a db healthcheck and (in compose v2.1+ semantics) condition: service_healthy, or make the app retry connections
depends_on is broken — remove it
Add restart: always to the DB — that makes it ready faster
depends_on waits for TCP readiness by default — the app has a bug
scenarios.why: depends_on only controls start order. Readiness needs a healthcheck (e.g., pg_isready) on db plus 'condition: service_healthy' — supported in classic compose file formats (note: compose spec v2 dropped long-form conditions; healthcheck-based waiting is handled via depends_on + healthcheck in current Docker Compose). The robust app-side fix is retry-with-backoff on connect — ordering can never fully replace resilience.
scenarios.hint: Does 'started' mean 'ready to accept connections'?

scenarios.title: Secrets in the compose file
scenarios.situation: The compose file hardcodes POSTGRES_PASSWORD=hunter2. It's committed to git and shared with contractors.
scenarios.prompt: What are the proper ways to inject it?
choices: env_file: .env (gitignored) or environment: with ${POSTGRES_PASSWORD} interpolation from the shell — never commit secrets
It's fine — compose files aren't sensitive
Base64 the password in the file — that's encryption
Put the password in the image instead — images aren't shared
scenarios.why: env_file loads a gitignored .env; ${VAR} interpolates from the shell environment (with ${VAR:-default} fallbacks). Either keeps secrets out of version control. For stronger needs: Docker Swarm/compose 'secrets:' mounts secrets as files. Images are shared artifacts — baking secrets into them is worse, not better.
scenarios.hint: Where should the secret live so git never sees it?

scenarios.title: The database vanished
scenarios.situation: You ran 'docker compose down -v' to 'clean up', then 'up' again — the database is empty. Your teammate is upset.
scenarios.prompt: What did -v do, and how do you avoid it?
choices: -v removes named volumes declared in the compose file — plain 'down' keeps them; only use -v when you truly want data destroyed
-v means verbose — it just printed more output
down always deletes volumes — data loss was unavoidable
Volumes are never deleted — the DB must have failed differently
scenarios.why: 'docker compose down' stops and removes containers/networks but preserves named volumes (your data survives). '-v/--volumes' explicitly deletes them — the 'nuke the data' option. Anonymous volumes are removed by default on down. Lesson: know what -v destroys before typing it near production-like data.
scenarios.hint: Which flag is the difference between 'stop everything' and 'destroy the data too'?

scenarios.title: Dev vs prod compose
scenarios.situation: Dev needs debug ports and volume-mounted source code; prod needs replicas and no debug. You don't want two divergent files.
scenarios.prompt: How do you layer the differences?
choices: Base compose.yaml plus compose.override.yaml (auto-merged) or -f compose.yaml -f compose.prod.yaml — later files merge/override
Copy the file per environment and edit — divergence is fine
Environment variables can't change compose behavior
Compose doesn't support multiple files
scenarios.why: Compose merges multiple -f files (later wins on conflicts; lists like ports merge). Convention: compose.yaml (base) + compose.override.yaml (auto-loaded for local dev tweaks) + explicit -f for prod. Combined with ${VAR} interpolation and profiles, one base serves all environments without duplication.
scenarios.hint: What happens when you pass two -f files with conflicting values?

scenarios.title: Service name as hostname
scenarios.situation: The app connects to 'postgres://db:5432/app'. There's no /etc/hosts entry and no external DNS — yet it resolves.
scenarios.prompt: Why?
choices: Compose creates a user-defined network with embedded DNS — every service is reachable by its service name
Docker edits the host's /etc/hosts automatically
db resolves via the internet DNS
It doesn't resolve — the app is misconfigured
scenarios.why: Each compose project gets a user-defined bridge network with an embedded DNS server: service names (and container names) resolve to container IPs, with basic load balancing across replicas. This is why inter-service communication 'just works' by service name — and why the legacy default bridge (no DNS) is inferior.
scenarios.hint: What provides DNS on a user-defined network that the default bridge lacks?

scenarios.title: Compose Service Ordering
scenarios.situation: A Compose stack's `web` service crashes on startup because the `db` service isn't accepting connections yet. `depends_on: [db]` is already set.
scenarios.prompt: What actually fixes the startup race?
evidence:
services:
  web:
    depends_on: [db]
    command: node server.js
  db:
    image: postgres:16
choices: Add a healthcheck to `db` and use `depends_on` with `condition: service_healthy`, plus retry logic in the app — `depends_on` only orders container start, not service readiness
Change to `depends_on: {db: {condition: service_started}}`; the long syntax makes the database start faster
Add `restart: always` to web and accept the crash loop as normal
Put both services in one container so they start together
scenarios.why: `depends_on` only guarantees start order, not readiness — the db container can be 'started' while Postgres is still initializing. The Compose healthcheck + `service_healthy` condition waits until the database actually accepts connections, and app-level retries cover the remaining race. This is the documented pattern for startup ordering.
scenarios.hint: The database container started — but was the database inside it ready? What does `depends_on` actually wait for?

scenarios.title: The app needs the host's network
scenarios.situation: A monitoring agent must see the host's network interfaces and use host ports directly. The default bridge network hides the host interfaces.
scenarios.prompt: Which network mode fits, and what do you lose?
choices: --network host — the container shares the host's network stack; you lose port mapping and network isolation
--network bridge with -p — identical to host mode
--network none — most performant option
Host mode doesn't exist on Linux — use macvlan
scenarios.why: host mode removes network isolation: the container sees host interfaces and binds host ports directly (no -p needed/possible). Use for network-monitoring agents or extreme-performance needs. You lose port mapping, DNS-per-network, and inter-container isolation — don't use it for regular apps. (Note: host networking doesn't work on Docker Desktop the same way.)
scenarios.hint: Which mode gives the container the host's own network stack?

scenarios.title: Connection refused from outside
scenarios.situation: The container runs the app on port 80 (verified via docker exec + curl localhost). From the host, 'curl localhost:8080' fails though you ran '-p 8080:80'.
scenarios.prompt: What are the likely causes?
choices: The app binds 127.0.0.1 inside the container (unreachable from outside its netns) — bind 0.0.0.0; or the -p flag order is reversed (host:container)
-p is broken — use --expose instead
Port 8080 is privileged — use a port below 1024
Containers can't receive external connections — by design
scenarios.why: Two classic causes: (1) the app listens on 127.0.0.1 inside its own network namespace — publish forwards to the container IP, not its loopback, so the app must bind 0.0.0.0; (2) -p syntax is host:container — reversed gives the wrong mapping. Diagnose: 'docker port <c>', 'ss -tlnp' on host, and check the app's bind address in logs.
scenarios.hint: From the host's perspective, which address does the published port forward to?

scenarios.title: Containers can't find each other
scenarios.situation: Two containers on the default bridge network can't resolve each other by name. The same setup on a custom network works.
scenarios.prompt: Why the difference?
choices: The default bridge has no embedded DNS (use IPs or legacy --link); user-defined networks provide automatic DNS resolution by container name
DNS is broken in Docker — use hostnames file mounts
Custom networks disable DNS — the working setup is a fluke
Container names are random — they can't be resolved
scenarios.why: User-defined networks get an embedded DNS server resolving container names/aliases; the legacy default bridge doesn't (a historical limitation — --link was the old workaround, now deprecated). Best practice: always create explicit networks ('docker network create appnet') and attach containers to them.
scenarios.hint: Which network type did Docker add DNS to?

scenarios.title: Which container has which IP?
scenarios.situation: Debugging connectivity: you need each container's IP, its networks, and published ports in one view.
scenarios.prompt: Which commands give you this?
choices: docker network inspect <net> (per-network members + IPs) and docker inspect <container> (networks, ports, IPAM details)
docker ps — shows full networking details
ifconfig on the host — lists container IPs
Container IPs are unknowable — they're internal
scenarios.why: 'docker network inspect' shows all attached containers with their IPv4/IPv6 addresses and aliases; 'docker inspect' gives the container's NetworkSettings (per-network IPs, port bindings, DNS). 'docker ps' shows published ports but not internal IPs. For name resolution testing: 'docker exec <c> getent hosts <name>'.
scenarios.hint: Which inspect target shows the network's member list with IPs?

scenarios.title: The container needs a LAN IP
scenarios.situation: A legacy app must appear as a physical host on the office LAN (its license is MAC-bound, and peers expect it on 192.168.1.0/24).
scenarios.prompt: Which driver gives the container its own MAC and LAN IP?
choices: macvlan — attaches containers directly to the physical network with their own MAC/IP, appearing as physical hosts
bridge — with enough port mappings it looks physical
host — gives a LAN IP automatically
overlay — spans the LAN across hosts
scenarios.why: macvlan creates sub-interfaces on the parent NIC, each with its own MAC — containers get real LAN IPs via the physical network (DHCP or static). Trade-offs: needs promiscuous mode on the parent, containers can't talk to the host itself without a macvlan shim, and it bypasses Docker's port mapping. It's the escape hatch for legacy/physical-network requirements.
scenarios.hint: Which driver makes the container look like another physical machine on the switch?

scenarios.title: No network at all
scenarios.situation: A batch crypto-signing job must be airtight: it processes sensitive keys and should have zero network access, not even loopback surprises.
scenarios.prompt: How do you run it fully isolated?
choices: docker run --network none — the container gets only a loopback interface, no external connectivity
Don't publish ports — unpublished containers have no network
Use the default bridge — it's isolated enough
Air-gapping isn't possible — containers always have network
scenarios.why: --network none gives the container a network namespace containing only lo — no eth0, no routes out. Unpublished ports still leave full outbound connectivity (containers can reach the internet via NAT by default), so 'no -p' is not isolation. none is the true air-gap for sensitive batch work.
scenarios.hint: Does 'no published ports' also block outbound connections?

scenarios.title: Can't Reach the Other Container
scenarios.situation: Two containers on the default bridge network: the app tries to reach the database at `localhost:5432` and gets connection refused. Both containers are running.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct fix?
evidence:
NETWORK ID   NAME      DRIVER
abc123       bridge    bridge
choices: Put both containers on a user-defined network (or use Compose, which creates one) and connect via the container name as hostname — `localhost` inside a container refers to itself, not the database container
Publish the database port with `-p 5432:5432` and keep using localhost from the app
Run the database with `--network host` so it shares localhost with everything
Add `--link db` — the modern replacement for container DNS
scenarios.why: Each container has its own network namespace: `localhost` in the app container is the app container itself. On a user-defined bridge network, Docker provides embedded DNS so containers resolve each other by name (`db:5432`). Publishing ports helps host→container access, not container→container. `--link` is legacy.
scenarios.hint: Whose `localhost` is the app talking to — its own, or the database's?

scenarios.title: Swarm Loses Its Mind
scenarios.situation: A 5-manager Swarm cluster loses 3 managers to a network partition. The remaining 2 managers stop scheduling and the cluster goes read-only.
scenarios.prompt: Why did 2 surviving managers stop working, and what is the correct manager topology?
evidence: 2 managers alive but cluster frozen; `docker service ls` hangs
choices: Swarm uses Raft: it needs a majority (quorum) of managers — 3 of 5. With only 2 reachable, the cluster can't elect a leader and freezes to protect consistency; run an odd number of managers (3 or 5) spread across failure domains, and never let a partition take the majority
Swarm needs all managers alive; add more managers (7+) so some can fail
The 2 survivors should have force-elected a leader with `docker swarm init --force-new-cluster` immediately
Managers are stateless; the freeze is a bug — restart the daemon on the survivors
scenarios.why: Raft consensus requires (n/2)+1 managers. 5 managers tolerate 2 failures; losing 3 kills quorum and the cluster correctly freezes rather than split-brain. The fix is topological: odd manager count across AZs, and `--force-new-cluster` only as a last-resort recovery, not routine.
scenarios.hint: How many managers must agree to elect a leader out of 5?

scenarios.title: Services Can't Find Each Other
scenarios.situation: Two services on the same user-defined overlay network resolve each other by name, but after moving one service to the default `bridge` network, name resolution breaks.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct explanation and fix?
evidence:
overlay net: app-net (2 services attached)
bridge: 1 service (moved)
choices: Docker's embedded DNS (127.0.0.11) provides service discovery only on user-defined networks; the default bridge network has no embedded DNS — put both services on the same user-defined (overlay) network
Add `--dns 8.8.8.8` to the moved container; external DNS resolves Swarm names
Restart the Docker daemon to rebuild the DNS cache
Overlay networks don't support DNS; use static IPs in both services
scenarios.why: Embedded DNS with automatic service discovery is a feature of user-defined networks (bridge or overlay), not the legacy default bridge. On an overlay, every service gets a VIP/DNS entry. Moving a service to the default bridge strands it without name resolution.
scenarios.hint: Which networks get the 127.0.0.11 embedded DNS server?

scenarios.title: Database storage choice
scenarios.situation: Postgres runs in a container. You need its data to survive container replacement, perform well, and be portable across hosts.
scenarios.prompt: Named volume or bind mount — and why?
choices: Named volume — managed by Docker, portable, correct permissions/SELinux handling, survives container removal; bind mounts tie you to host paths
Bind mount — volumes are slower
Neither — databases can't run in containers
tmpfs — fastest option for databases
scenarios.why: Named volumes (docker volume create pgdata; -v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data) are Docker-managed: portable across hosts, work with volume drivers (NFS, cloud), get proper ownership handling, and persist independent of container lifecycle. Bind mounts (-v /host/path:/container/path) couple you to host paths and UID quirks — fine for dev config injection, wrong for production data.
scenarios.hint: Which option keeps working when you move to a different host?

scenarios.title: Permission denied on the bind mount
scenarios.situation: You bind-mount ./data into the container. The app (running as UID 1000) gets 'permission denied' — the host directory is owned by root.
scenarios.prompt: What are the fixes?
choices: chown the host dir to the container user's UID, or run the container with --user matching the host owner — bind mounts preserve host UID/GID semantics
chmod 777 ./data — the standard fix
Bind mounts can't do permissions — switch to tmpfs
Run everything as root — UIDs don't matter in containers
scenarios.why: Bind mounts expose host files with host ownership — the container's UID 1000 is the host's UID 1000. Fixes: chown 1000:1000 ./data on the host, or 'docker run --user $(id -u):$(id -g)'. Named volumes avoid this (Docker initializes ownership). 777 'works' by abandoning all access control — never in production.
scenarios.hint: Is UID 1000 in the container a different user than UID 1000 on the host?

scenarios.title: Backing up the named volume
scenarios.situation: The pgdata volume holds production data. You need a backup to S3 nightly — but you can't just copy from the host path reliably while Postgres runs.
scenarios.prompt: What is the safe backup pattern?
choices: Run a temporary container with --volumes-from (or -v pgdata:/data) that streams a consistent backup (pg_dump / tar) to S3 — never copy live DB files raw
docker cp the volume directory while Postgres runs — files are consistent
Volumes back up automatically — nothing to do
Stop Docker entirely for the backup window
scenarios.why: Attach a helper container to the volume ('docker run --rm -v pgdata:/data -v $(pwd):/backup alpine tar czf /backup/pg.tar.gz /data') for file-level backup, or better: pg_dump from a linked container for a consistent logical backup. Raw-copying live database files risks corruption — use the DB's own tools. Restore is the reverse mount.
scenarios.hint: What makes a database backup consistent that a file copy isn't?

scenarios.title: Config that must not change
scenarios.situation: You mount a config file into the container. A bug in the app overwrote it last week, breaking the host's copy too.
scenarios.prompt: How do you mount it safely?
choices: -v ./config.yaml:/app/config.yaml:ro — the read-only flag prevents container writes from affecting the host file
Config files can't be protected — that's normal
Copy the file in instead of mounting — mounts are always writable
:ro only works for named volumes, not bind mounts
scenarios.why: The :ro suffix (or --mount type=bind,source=...,target=...,readonly) mounts read-only — the container physically cannot modify it. Use for configs, certificates, and any host file the container should never change. Defense in depth alongside running as non-root.
scenarios.hint: Which mount option makes the container's view read-only?

scenarios.title: Mystery volumes piling up
scenarios.situation: 'docker volume ls' shows dozens of hash-named volumes. They came from a Dockerfile VOLUME instruction; 'docker compose down' didn't remove them.
scenarios.prompt: What are these, and how do you avoid the pileup?
choices: Anonymous volumes — created implicitly by VOLUME instructions; 'down -v' removes them, but better to declare named volumes explicitly in compose
They're a bug — Docker shouldn't create volumes unprompted
Anonymous volumes are deleted automatically — just wait
VOLUME instructions are comments — these came from elsewhere
scenarios.why: Dockerfile VOLUME creates an anonymous volume at each container creation if no explicit mount is given — they accumulate because nothing references them by name. Fixes: mount named volumes explicitly (overrides the anonymous one), and clean up with 'docker volume prune' (careful — removes ALL unused volumes). Prefer explicit named volumes in compose files.
scenarios.hint: What creates a volume when the Dockerfile says VOLUME but nothing is mounted?

scenarios.title: -v or --mount?
scenarios.situation: Your team mixes '-v pgdata:/data:ro' and '--mount type=volume,source=pgdata,target=/data,readonly'. A newcomer asks which to standardize on.
scenarios.prompt: What is the guidance?
choices: --mount is explicit and verbose (fails clearly on missing fields); -v is terse but its positional fields are error-prone — prefer --mount in scripts/docs, -v for interactive use
-v is deprecated — never use it
--mount can't do read-only — use -v
They're identical in every way — no guidance needed
scenarios.why: --mount's key=value syntax is self-documenting and validates (e.g., refuses a bind mount to a nonexistent source unless created). -v's positional 'src:dst:opts' is compact but easy to misorder (swapped source/target is a classic bug). Both work everywhere; --mount is the safer default for anything committed to a repo.
scenarios.hint: Which syntax makes a swapped source/target obvious?

scenarios.title: Data Vanished with the Container
scenarios.situation: A developer ran a database in a container, stopped it, removed it, and started a fresh one — all the data is gone.
scenarios.prompt: What should they have done?
evidence:
docker run -d --name db postgres:16
docker stop db && docker rm db
docker run -d --name db postgres:16  # data gone
choices: Mount a named volume or host directory at the data path (e.g., `-v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data`) so data lives outside the container's writable layer and survives container replacement
Use `docker pause` instead of `docker stop` so the container is never removed
Commit the running container to a new image before stopping; committed images include the data
Run the database with `--restart always`; restarted containers keep their data
scenarios.why: A container's writable layer dies with the container — `docker rm` destroys it. Persistent data must live in a volume (managed by Docker) or a bind mount (a host path), both of which outlive any single container. `commit` bakes data into an image, which is an anti-pattern for databases; `--restart` only helps if the container is never removed.
scenarios.hint: When the container is deleted, which storage disappears with it — and which storage is designed to outlive it?

scenarios.title: The Disk Ate the Logs
scenarios.situation: A long-running container's `json-file` logs grew unbounded and filled the host disk, crashing the daemon. `docker logs` on the box is now unusable.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct log hygiene?
choices: Configure log rotation in `daemon.json` (`log-opts: {"max-size": "10m", "max-file": "3"}`) or per-container `--log-opt`, and ship logs to a central aggregator instead of keeping them on the host forever
Run `docker logs --tail` more often to keep the file small
Delete the json.log file while the container runs; the daemon recreates it empty
Switch to `--log-driver none`; logs are expendable
scenarios.why: json-file logging is unbounded by default — every stdout line appends forever. max-size/max-file gives bounded local retention; the durable answer is shipping to a log aggregator (ELK/Loki/CloudWatch). Deleting an open log file doesn't free the space until the writer closes it.
scenarios.hint: Who writes that json.log file, and does it ever stop growing on its own?

scenarios.title: Running as non-root
scenarios.situation: Your Dockerfile ends with the app running as root. The image runs fine, but the security team rejects it.
scenarios.prompt: What is the proper fix in the Dockerfile?
choices: Create a user (RUN useradd/groupadd or use the base image's), chown the app files, and set USER appuser — numeric UID preferred
Add USER at the top — it applies retroactively
Running as root in containers is safe — push back on security
USER nobody — always exists and owns everything
scenarios.why: USER switches the runtime user for subsequent instructions and the container process. Create a dedicated user, ensure it owns what it needs (chown in the same layer), prefer numeric UIDs (name resolution isn't guaranteed at runtime). Combined with dropping capabilities and read-only filesystems, this is container hardening 101.
scenarios.hint: Which instruction changes the user — and what must be true about file ownership?

scenarios.title: Secrets in ENV
scenarios.situation: The Dockerfile has 'ENV DB_PASSWORD=hunter2'. The password is now in the image layers, visible via 'docker history' and to anyone who pulls the image.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct way to provide secrets to containers?
choices: Inject at runtime: -e from a protected source, env_file (gitignored), Docker secrets (swarm), or orchestrator secret mounts — never bake into layers
ENV is fine — layers are encrypted
Use ARG instead — build args don't persist
Base64 the ENV value — that's the fix
scenarios.why: ENV values persist in image config/history forever — anyone with the image has the secret. ARG is also visible in history. Runtime injection (-e, --env-file, compose env_file, secrets mounted as files) keeps secrets out of the artifact. For CI: secret managers or masked CI variables, never committed files.
scenarios.hint: Who can read an image's ENV values?

scenarios.title: CVE in the base image
scenarios.situation: Your scanner flags a critical CVE in the base image's OpenSSL. The app doesn't use TLS directly, but the library is present.
scenarios.prompt: What is the remediation workflow?
choices: Rebuild on a patched base image tag (or minimal alternative), rescan, and add scanning as a CI gate so it fails before merge next time
Ignore it — the app doesn't use OpenSSL
Scanners produce false positives — disable scanning
Patch the running container with apt-get — persistent fix
scenarios.why: Presence = exposure (attackers find paths you didn't). Remediation: bump the base (patched tag or slim/distroless alternative), rebuild, rescan to verify. CI gates ('docker scout cves' / Trivy / Grype failing on critical) prevent regressions. Patching running containers is ephemeral — the next deploy reintroduces the CVE.
scenarios.hint: Where does the permanent fix live — the running container or the build?

scenarios.title: Hardening the runtime flags
scenarios.situation: You run a stateless API container with default flags. Hardening review asks for the standard runtime restrictions.
scenarios.prompt: Which flags form the baseline?
choices: --read-only (immutable fs; tmpfs mounts for /tmp), --cap-drop ALL --cap-add as needed, --user, --memory/--cpus limits, --pids-limit
--privileged — required for hardening tools to work
Defaults are already hardened — no flags needed
--cap-add ALL — capabilities improve security
scenarios.why: Runtime hardening stack: --read-only (with --tmpfs for scratch), --cap-drop ALL + minimal adds, --user (non-root), resource limits (--memory, --cpus, --pids-limit to bound DoS/blast radius), --security-opt no-new-privileges. Each shrinks what a compromised container can do. --privileged is the opposite of hardening.
scenarios.hint: Which flags reduce what a compromised container can do?

scenarios.title: Blocking setuid escalation
scenarios.situation: A container runs a legacy binary with the setuid bit. If exploited, the process could escalate within the container.
scenarios.prompt: Which flag blocks privilege escalation via setuid?
choices: --security-opt no-new-privileges:true — the kernel blocks setuid/setgid privilege gains for the container's processes
--cap-drop SETUID — capabilities control this
Remove the binary — the only fix
setuid doesn't work in containers — no action needed
scenarios.why: no-new-privileges is a kernel flag preventing processes from gaining privileges via setuid/setgid binaries or file capabilities — a cheap, powerful containment control. Combine with dropping capabilities and non-root USER. It's part of the default Docker seccomp/AppArmor story but worth setting explicitly in security-sensitive contexts.
scenarios.hint: Which kernel-level flag neuters setuid inside the container?

scenarios.title: Proving the image is yours
scenarios.situation: Anyone can push to your registry namespace (misconfigured). You need consumers to verify images actually came from your CI.
scenarios.prompt: What provides verifiable provenance?
choices: Sign images in CI (cosign/Sigstore) and verify signatures (or attestations/SLSA) at deploy time with admission policy
Tags prove provenance — only CI knows the tag
Registries sign automatically — nothing to do
Rename images frequently — attackers can't track them
scenarios.why: Signing (cosign with Sigstore keyless: OIDC identity from CI) attaches verifiable signatures + attestations (SLSA provenance: what source, what build). Deploy-time verification (Kyverno/Connaisseur admission, or 'cosign verify' in pipelines) rejects unsigned/forged images. Fix the registry RBAC too — signing complements access control, doesn't replace it.
scenarios.hint: What cryptographically ties an image to the CI run that built it?

scenarios.title: The API Key in the Image
scenarios.situation: A deploy fails security review: the production image contains a cloud API key baked in via `ENV API_KEY=...` in the Dockerfile, and the key is now in the registry forever.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct secrets handling for Swarm and for builds?
evidence: ENV API_KEY=sk-live-abc123  # baked into layer history
docker history shows the ENV layer with the value
choices: Remove the key from the Dockerfile; pass secrets at runtime via `docker secret` (mounted at /run/secrets in Swarm) or BuildKit secret mounts (`--mount=type=secret`) so they never land in layers or the registry
Keep the ENV but add the Dockerfile to .dockerignore
Encode the key in base64 in the ENV; it's no longer plaintext
Push the image to a private registry; baked-in keys are fine if the registry is private
scenarios.why: Anything in a Dockerfile layer is permanent history — registries, caches, and `docker history` all expose it. Runtime secrets (Swarm secrets, Kubernetes Secrets, BuildKit secret mounts) keep values out of layers. Base64 is encoding, not protection.
scenarios.hint: Once it's in a layer, where does that layer live forever?

scenarios.title: Who Built This Image?
scenarios.situation: After a supply-chain scare, policy requires that only signed images from the CI pipeline can be deployed. `docker pull` currently accepts anything with the right name.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct mechanism?
evidence: a typosquatted image with a similar name was deployed to staging
choices: Enable Docker Content Trust (`DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST=1`): pulls/pushes are verified against Notary signatures, so only images signed by trusted keys (e.g. the CI publisher key) are accepted
Rely on image digests alone; digests prove authorship
Scan images with a vulnerability scanner; scanning replaces signing
Pin tags to `latest`; mutable tags are always trustworthy
scenarios.why: Content Trust (Notary/TUF) binds an image to a publisher's signature — the client verifies provenance before running anything. Digests prove integrity (the bits didn't change) but say nothing about who produced them. Scanning finds CVEs; it doesn't authenticate the publisher.
scenarios.hint: What's the difference between 'these bits are unchanged' and 'I know who made these bits'?

scenarios.title: The Images & Dockerfiles Mystery

scenarios.prompt: Using the systems anatomy method (whole → cut open → step through → pull apart), how would you systematically trace a failure in Images & Dockerfiles?
choices: Walk the full journey: start from the trigger, verify each handoff in sequence, check dependencies at every step, and isolate where the flow breaks — then examine that specific layer
Restart all components — Images & Dockerfiles issues are always fixed by restarting
Check the most common cause from memory and apply that fix immediately
Escalate to senior support — Images & Dockerfiles is too complex to troubleshoot systematically
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Systems thinking means tracing the living flow: (1) Whole: what is Images & Dockerfiles supposed to do end-to-end? (2) Cut open: what are the layers/stages? (3) Step through: verify each handoff — where does the expected output diverge from actual? (4) Pull apart: isolate the broken layer and examine it in detail. This method works for any Images & Dockerfiles failure in Docker.
scenarios.hint: Don't jump to the fix. First map the journey, then find where it breaks.
objectives: Apply systems anatomy to Images & Dockerfiles
evidence: All Images & Dockerfiles components report 'online'. Basic health checks pass.
Functionality is broken despite green status indicators. The failure is in the flow, not the components.

lessons.title: Images & Dockerfiles — Core concepts
concepts: COPY vs ADD: best practice: COPY by default, ADD only when you need its extra behaviors (and even URL fetching is often clearer as an explicit RUN curl with checksum verification). Multi-stage builds let you use heavy tooling in an early stage and copy only artifacts into the final minimal stage (e.g., nginx:alpine).
CMD vs ENTRYPOINT: with exec-form ENTRYPOINT, 'docker run <image> <args>' appends <args> to the ENTRYPOINT — replacing CMD entirely.
Build cache: .dockerignore keeps unwanted files out of the build context (faster builds, smaller images, fewer leaks). Layer count barely matters; cache invalidation order is everything.

Layer ordering: deleting files in a later RUN doesn't shrink the image — the earlier layer still contains them. Docker caches each layer and invalidates everything after the first changed instruction.

example.code:
ENTRYPOINT ["python", "app.py", "--port", "8080"]
CMD ["--port", "8080"]
example.walkthrough: With exec-form ENTRYPOINT, 'docker run <image> <args>' appends <args> to the ENTRYPOINT — replacing CMD entirely. Here the final command becomes 'python app.py --port 8080 --port 9090', and the app takes the first flag. The idiomatic split: ENTRYPOINT ["python", "app.py"] (the fixed executable) + CMD ["--port", "8080"] (default args, overridable).

pitfalls: Common trap: combine COPY and RUN into a single layer to reduce layer count.
Common trap: docker run arguments override ENTRYPOINT, not CMD.
Common trap: CMD is ignored whenever ENTRYPOINT exists.
Common trap: add --no-cache to the build so layers are always fresh.

host networking: (Note: host networking doesn't work on Docker Desktop the same way.). Port publishing: diagnose: 'docker port <c>', 'ss -tlnp' on host, and check the app's bind address in logs. Trade-offs: needs promiscuous mode on the parent, containers can't talk to the host itself without a macvlan shim, and it bypasses Docker's port mapping.

lessons.title: How to Use This Bootcamp
concepts: The study order is deliberate — follow it: Start Here → core domains in sequence → Systems Anatomy → Mock Assessment → Capstone. Each module unlocks the next.
What 'terminal' means: a terminal (also called console or shell) is a text window where you type commands. This bootcamp has a built-in simulated terminal — use it for every hands-on lesson.
The interview strategy: learn concepts first (lessons), apply them under realistic conditions (scenarios), prove hands-on skill (labs), then validate under pressure (mock assessment).
Progress is saved automatically. A lesson completes only after you pass its knowledge check — this verifies real understanding, not just clicking through.
Scenarios are decision exercises: read the situation, review evidence, choose the best action. Wrong answers teach as much as right ones — read every explanation.
Labs are guided hands-on builds. Follow each step, verify with the checks, and don't skip the 'try it' extensions.

Your path through Docker:

  1. START HERE (this domain) — learn how to learn
  2. CORE DOMAINS — lessons + scenarios + labs, in order
  3. SYSTEMS ANATOMY — see how it all moves together
  4. MOCK ASSESSMENT — timed, exam-realistic, no hints
  5. CAPSTONE — build something real to prove it

Scenarios in this bootcamp mirror real incidents and decisions — the same shape as interview questions and exam case studies.
The capstone project gives you a portfolio artifact: something you can demo, link on your resume, and discuss confidently.
Systems Anatomy teaches you to narrate how systems work as living flows — the single biggest differentiator in technical interviews.

lessons.title: How Docker Actually Works
concepts: The daemon (dockerd) does the work; the CLI is just a client talking over a socket — you can even drive it via API
Namespaces isolate (pid, net, mnt...), cgroups limit (CPU, memory) — containers are processes with boundaries, not VMs
The storage driver layers images as diffs; copy-on-write means containers start fast and share base layers
docker inspect is the truth serum: when behavior confuses you, inspect the container's actual config

example.code:
$ docker inspect <container> | jq '.[0].Mounts, .[0].NetworkSettings'
$ ls /proc/<pid>/ns  # namespaces of a container process
example.walkthrough: Run a container, find its PID, and list its namespaces. Compare with a host process.

pitfalls: 'Docker is a lightweight VM' — no: shared kernel, process isolation, fundamentally different
Ignoring the daemon logs — dockerd tells you why builds/pulls fail
Assuming containers are secure by default — they're isolated, not hardened
lessons.try_it: Inspect 3 running containers. For each, identify its mounts, network mode, and resource limits.

lessons.title: Images as Layered Filesystems
concepts: Each Dockerfile instruction creates a layer; layers are content-addressed and shared across images
Layer order matters: put infrequently-changing steps first for cache hits
docker history shows each layer's size and command — use it to find bloat
Multi-arch images (amd64/arm64) via buildx — your M1-built image fails on x86 servers without this

example.code:
$ docker history myapp:latest
$ docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 -t myapp:1.0 .
example.walkthrough: Run docker history on an image. Identify the 3 largest layers and propose how to shrink each.

pitfalls: One giant RUN layer to 'reduce layers' — destroys cache granularity
Secrets in layers — every layer is retrievable; use build secrets
Not pinning base image digests — 'it worked yesterday' mysteries
lessons.try_it: Rebuild an image optimizing layer order. Measure build time on a no-op rebuild (cache efficiency).

lessons.title: Multi-Stage Build Patterns
concepts: Builder stage: full toolchain, compiles artifacts. Runtime stage: minimal base + artifacts only
COPY --from=builder selects exactly what crosses stages — nothing else leaks through
Distroless/scratch bases for static binaries; alpine for dynamic — smallest attack surface that still runs
Named stages + --target let you build test/debug variants from the same Dockerfile

example.code:
FROM golang:1.22 AS build
WORKDIR /src
COPY . .
RUN go build -o /app .
FROM gcr.io/distroless/static
COPY --from=build /app /app
ENTRYPOINT ["/app"]
example.walkthrough: Convert a single-stage Dockerfile to multi-stage. Compare sizes and list what got excluded.

pitfalls: COPY --from without stage name clarity — brittle when stages reorder
Debugging distroless with no shell — keep a debug target with busybox
Build secrets via COPY — use --mount=type=secret instead
lessons.try_it: Add a 'debug' target to your Dockerfile with shell + tools. Build both targets.

lessons.title: From Compose to Swarm
concepts: Compose defines multi-container apps for one host; Swarm schedules them across hosts — same file, bigger stage
Services (not containers) are the unit in Swarm: desired state, replicated, self-healing
Overlays network containers across hosts; ingress load-balances published ports
docker stack deploy turns your compose file into a distributed deployment

example.code:
$ docker swarm init
$ docker stack deploy -c compose.yml myapp
$ docker service ls  # desired vs actual state
example.walkthrough: Take a compose file, init a single-node swarm, deploy as a stack. Scale a service and watch rescheduling.

pitfalls: Compose-isms that don't translate: build: contexts, certain volume drivers
No placement constraints — stateful services landing on random nodes
Forgetting swarm needs odd managers for quorum — 2 managers is worse than 1
lessons.try_it: Simulate a node failure (stop the daemon). Observe and document the rescheduling behavior.

lessons.title: Systematic Docker Debugging
concepts: Order: docker ps (is it running?) → logs (what's it saying?) → inspect (what's it configured as?) → exec (what's happening inside?)
docker events streams the daemon's view — container deaths, OOM kills, and network changes in real time
dive (third-party) shows layer-by-layer filesystem — find what's bloating or missing
Reproduce minimally: strip the compose file to one service, then add back until it breaks

example.code:
$ docker events --filter container=myapp &
$ docker logs --tail 50 -f myapp
$ docker exec -it myapp sh  # what's actually in there?
example.walkthrough: Break a container 3 ways (bad env, missing volume, wrong port). Diagnose each with the systematic order.

pitfalls: Reading app logs when it's a platform issue — check events and daemon first
latest-tag confusion — 'it works locally' with a stale cached image
Not checking disk — 'no space left' from dangling images/volumes is embarrassingly common
lessons.try_it: Run docker system df. Reclaim space with prune. Document what each prune variant removes.

lessons.title: Docker Projects That Demonstrate Skill
concepts: Project 1: multi-service app (API + DB + cache) with compose, healthchecks, and resource limits
Project 2: hardened production image — distroless, non-root, scanned, signed, with SBOM
READMEs must include: architecture diagram, how to run (one command), and security decisions
CI that builds, scans, and pushes on every commit — containers without pipelines are just tarballs

example.code:
One-command run:
$ git clone ... && docker compose up
# working in < 2 minutes, documented ports/creds
example.walkthrough: Score your docker project: one-command run? pinned digests? non-root? scan clean? SBOM?

pitfalls: 'docker run' commands in README instead of compose — not reproducible
No .dockerignore — build contexts with .git and node_modules
Screenshots instead of a runnable project — must be clone-and-run
lessons.try_it: Add image scanning to your project's CI. Fix every HIGH/CRITICAL finding or document why not.

simulations.brief: A container exits immediately with code 1. The image was rebuilt this morning.
simulations.debrief: Exit 1 on start = the container's command fails. Read the logs — they carry the app's own error. Common causes: missing env var, wrong CMD, config file not found. The fix is in the image or the run flags, not in restarting.

simulations.debrief: Volumes persist data beyond container life; bind mounts share host files (like config) into the container. Data that must survive: named volumes. Config you edit: bind mounts. Never bake either into the image.

simulations.debrief: Base image first, then dependencies (the slow-changing layers, cached), then the app code, then the runtime config (ports, CMD). Layer order is a caching strategy: stable layers at the top.

simulations.brief: This Dockerfile is headed for production. Click the misconfigured lines (2 issues to find).
simulations.debrief: Two production mistakes: running as root (a container escape becomes host root — add a USER), and COPY . . after dependency install busting the layer cache on every code change. Order layers by change frequency; drop privileges.

steps.config:
FROM python:3.12-slim
RUN pip install flask gunicorn
COPY . /app
CMD ["gunicorn", "app:app"]

issues.description: No USER instruction — the container runs as root.
issues.fix: Create a non-root user and add USER appuser before CMD.

issues.description: COPY . /app after dependency install means every code change invalidates the cache... (here deps and code are fused — split requirements install before the code copy).
issues.fix: COPY requirements first, RUN pip install, then COPY the code.

Build cache — .dockerignore keeps unwanted files out of the build context (faster builds, smaller images, fewer leaks). Layer count barely matters; cache invalidation order is everything.

items: Network modes — 'docker network inspect' shows all attached containers with their IPv4/IPv6 addresses and aliases; 'docker inspect' gives the container's NetworkSettings (per-network IPs, port bindings, DNS).

Port publishing — diagnose: 'docker port <c>', 'ss -tlnp' on host, and check the app's bind address in logs. Trade-offs: needs promiscuous mode on the parent, containers can't talk to the host itself without a macvlan shim, and it bypasses Docker's port mapping.

User-defined networks — best practice: always create explicit networks ('docker network create appnet') and attach containers to them.

sections.heading: Volumes
items: Bind mounts (-v /host/path — /container/path) couple you to host paths and UID quirks — fine for dev config injection, wrong for production data. Bind mounts expose host files with host ownership — the container's UID 1000 is the host's UID 1000.
Volumes — fixes: mount named volumes explicitly (overrides the anonymous one), and clean up with 'docker volume prune' (careful — removes ALL unused volumes).
Volume sharing — dockerfile VOLUME creates an anonymous volume at each container creation if no explicit mount is given — they accumulate because nothing references them by name.
Read-only mounts — the :ro suffix (or --mount type=bind,source=...,target=...,readonly) mounts read-only — the container physically cannot modify it.
Common trap — :ro only works for named volumes, not bind mounts.
Common trap — anonymous volumes are deleted automatically.
Common trap — docker cp the volume directory while Postgres runs.
Common trap — docker shouldn't create volumes unprompted.

Non-root containers — patching running containers is ephemeral — the next deploy reintroduces the CVE. Combine with dropping capabilities and non-root USER.
Secrets — runtime injection (-e, --env-file, compose env_file, secrets mounted as files) keeps secrets out of the artifact.
ENV values persist in image config/history forever — anyone with the image has the secret.
